Nice Weather: the product direction

Everything that decides what the product does, in one place. The sliders run the real calculation: the table recounts ten years of hourly weather (2016 to 2025) at 31 places as you drag, the same way the map will. Your taste is the default. Reply with what you'd change; anything you don't mention, I take as agreed.

Where on earth is best all year round?

The day runs from 10:00 to 21:00. It is a nice day when most of its daylight hours are t-shirt weather and it stays inside four limits: the walk home, humidity, rain and wind.

T-shirt weather

Feels like: in the sun when it's cool, in the shade when it's hot.

The walk home at 21:00

Feels like at 21:00.

Humidity

The day's average dew point. Higher is muggier.

Rain

The day's average; gusts run higher.

Each cell is the share of days that month that are nice. A grey figure after a year total is the change from your default taste. Corrected for coast and height: the twelve places you graded before, and San Francisco, which uses its downtown weather station. The rest, including the top four and San Diego and Los Angeles, use the raw 25 km weather data, which can read coastal places a few degrees off, so their order may still move.

At your taste, the places closest to SoCal at its best, all year, are the Canary Islands (Gran Canaria 281 nice days, south Tenerife 274) and high, dry cities in the tropics (Nairobi at 1,800 m: 254; Guadalajara at 1,550 m: 259): warm every afternoon and rarely muggy. San Diego gets 248 and Los Angeles 240. San Francisco, on real temperatures, gets 111. Honolulu falls to 170: its dew point sits around 20 to 21 °C from May to October. These are 31 places I picked; the map ranks every square on land, including places nobody thought of.

What the sliders mean

T-shirt weather
An hour counts when it feels at least the lower figure in the sun and at most the upper one in the shade, as you'd choose yourself. Colder doesn't count at all. Hotter fades out over 3 °C, because a bit too hot is easier to live with than a bit too cold. Only daylight hours up to 20:00 count; after dark, the walk home decides. For scale: Málaga at 13:00 in November feels 22 °C in the sun; Seville at 16:00 in July, 35 °C in the shade.
The walk home at 21:00
Colder, and it isn't a nice day. Walking warms you, so a t-shirt stays fine a few degrees cooler than sitting still. For scale: San Diego at 21:00 feels 11 °C in January (13 °C on the thermometer) and 25 °C in August; Málaga feels 14 °C in November.
Humidity
The day's average dew point, 10:00 to 21:00. More humid, and it isn't a nice day. Dew point measures the moisture in the air as a temperature: the higher, the muggier. Humidity in % is no use here: it falls as the day warms while the air stays just as muggy. For scale: Seville in July 15 °C, San Diego and Málaga in August 18 °C, Austin in July 21 °C, Singapore 24 °C all year.
Rain
Rain from 10:00 to 21:00. Wetter, and it isn't a nice day. Weather services call 1 mm or more a wet day: a short shower, or a couple of hours of drizzle. 5 mm is a few proper showers; 10 mm, a wet afternoon.
Wind
The day's average wind, 10:00 to 21:00; gusts run higher. Windier, and it isn't a nice day. Wind already counts in how warm it feels, so this limit is only for the nuisance: dust, sand, hair. For scale: Cape Town in January averages 25 km/h, and over 35 km/h on about one day in eight.
Feels like
The thermometer adjusted for humidity, wind and sun, by the formula Australia's weather service uses (Steadman's apparent temperature). On a calm, dry night it reads 2 to 3 °C below the thermometer; on a humid afternoon, several degrees above.
Grades
The forecast grades each day by its share of t-shirt hours: 55% or more is Nice, 70% Beautiful, 85% Perfect; below that, Fair, Poor or Awful. A day that breaks a limit is Fair at best. The table counts Nice or better.

With no humidity limit, Singapore still gets 94 days at 30 °C: on those, most daylight hours feel about 30 °C or less in the shade. The humidity limit is what rules it out, as it should, because muggy air is its own nuisance, not just heat. The settings in your screenshot (21 to 37 °C, 21:00 at least 19 °C, dew point 21 °C, no rain limit, wind 30 km/h) now give Singapore 1 nice day a year and Bangkok 50; before, 365 and 359.

You asked whether an average wind of 30 km/h should rule a day out. I've set the limit at 35 km/h. At 30, Cape Town loses a fifth of its summer days (61% nice instead of 78%), which doesn't fit your ranking of it as the best place in December to February.

I tested a sunshine minimum as another limit and left it out. It barely changes anything, because days warm enough for a t-shirt are almost always sunny.

Austin, where you just were

Austin gets 99 nice days a year at your taste, and you went in its best month. October: 56% of days nice, highs around 30 °C and still 24 °C at 21:00, t-shirt day and night. November: 41%, highs around 23 °C and 14 °C by 21:00. March and April come close to October (55% and 58%).

June to August is too hot and humid: 0 to 5% nice, still 33 °C at 21:00, with a dew point of 21 °C. December to February (9 to 28%) has highs of 17 to 20 °C and cold evenings.

You expected Austin in November to beat Málaga for t-shirt time. It doesn't: 41% of November days are nice in Austin and 47% in Málaga. Both feel about 14 °C by 21:00.

Why SoCal isn't nice all year

From June to October San Diego and Los Angeles are t-shirt weather nearly all day and 20 to 25 °C at 21:00. Winter is the gap. Middays are fine (San Diego at 13:00 in January feels 22 °C in the sun), but the sun sets around 17:00, the late afternoon turns cool, and 21:00 feels 11 °C. So December to February has 29 nice days out of 90 in San Diego and 26 in Los Angeles at your defaults. Rain on about one January day in ten does the rest. SoCal's winter is mild, sunny middays, not shorts all day.

Bay Area microclimates

They are large, and today's data barely sees them. On an average July afternoon Half Moon Bay is 17 °C, downtown San Francisco 19 °C, San Jose 28 °C and Livermore 32 °C. Each weather square is about 25 km across, too coarse to see a fog belt a few kilometres wide, so the data reads the foggy coast about 5 °C too warm and the inland valleys up to 4 °C too cold.

"Real temperatures" reshapes each day's hourly temperatures to that day's measured high and low at the station, 2016 to 2025. Sun, wind, humidity and rain stay as the weather data has them.

The fix is a fine climate map built from weather stations: PRISM, at 800 m, for the US. Each pixel's temperature is shifted by how much warmer or cooler that spot runs than its weather square, month by month. That gets every place to within 20 nice days a year of the real temperatures, against errors of up to 85 days today. Outside the US the same correction uses WorldClim, at about 1 km, as Theo's site does; I haven't tested that yet. One gap remains: fog also hides the sun, which a temperature map can't see, so the foggy coast may still read a little too nice.

So with real temperatures the Bay Area runs from about 100 nice days a year on the coast to about 200 in San Jose, against San Diego's 252. San Francisco in the table above uses the downtown station's real temperatures; fog hiding the sun probably takes a few more days off.

How the map keeps up with the sliders

Under 0.2 s for any change, anywhere on the map. Every 100 km square keeps a small sample of real days. When a slider moves, your device's graphics chip recounts them and adds the detail for height and coast pixel by pixel, the way Theo's map does. Rain, wind and humidity change slowly over distance, so 100 km is enough for them; temperature, which changes with every hill and coast, gets the pixel detail. Nothing waits on a server while you drag. Sites does the heavy work in advance: it builds the samples, and the map at your default taste in full detail, every day, so the first view is instant.

The small day summary this needs gives the same answer as the full hour-by-hour calculation, never more than 3 nice days a year apart at the 31 places (22 within 1). This page runs exactly that recount. The timing for the whole world on a phone is the first thing I measure when building.

What I'm fixing anyway

  • Coasts. Today coastal towns read 2 to 4 °C too cold, because each square mixes sea, coast and mountain. Taking temperature from the nearest land and correcting for height cuts the error to under 1 °C against weather stations. Cape Town still reads about 3 °C too hot in summer; that gets fixed before it goes live.
  • Rain. The data counts too many wet days in dry places: Málaga in January reads wet on 26% of days, its weather station 16.5%. I'll test Theo's correction against stations and keep whatever matches them.
  • Forecast and climate agree. Both use the same sun measure (from solar radiation) and the forecast adds gusts. 15 forecast days, as ECMWF gives; ECMWF's 9 km forecast when it becomes free.
  • The 20-year climate is built on Sites. It works; run one area at a time, the world would take weeks, so it runs in parallel.

Lock it

Decide 1: the walk home. You said it was penalised too much, and it was: the evening was judged twice, once as hours that had to be t-shirt weather and again by the 21:00 rule. Now only daylight hours count, and the evening is judged once, at 21:00, against a lower bar, because you are walking. Nice days at each setting:
